clue.text: Post-conceptual development more by accident

indicators.note: what happens by accident is unplanned, so the letters fall into a haphazard new order

blocks.note: the six letters taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone muses that, after the idea is conceived, further progress comes more through luck than planning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Post-conceptual' reads like art-world jargon about ideas; here it means after conception in the biological sense.
explanation.definitionFit: An embryo is the organism growing in the womb in the weeks after fertilisation, the first stage of development.

clue.text: Face down

blocks.note: surface reading: lying with the front turned towards the floor
setter's reading: the soft hair, or down, that grows on a man's face above the lip

explanation.walkthrough: Down here is fine hair, not a direction, so the phrase describes whiskers on the upper lip.
explanation.definitionFit: A moustache is hair growing on the upper lip, which the clue playfully calls the down of the face.

clue.text: This outlet sought by three blind mice?

definitions.note: read as a two-part verb, to put tails back on

blocks.note: first meaning: a shop selling direct to the public
second meaning: in the nursery rhyme the farmer's wife cut off the mice's tails, so they would want them fitted again

explanation.surface: A shop is being hunted for by the three blind mice of the nursery rhyme.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as RE-TAIL: the rhyme's mice lost their tails to a carving knife, so they would want them put back.
explanation.definitionFit: Retail is selling goods directly to the public, so a retail outlet is a shop or store.

clue.text: Put this to intrude with no one reason, perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps marks the letters as only one possible arrangement of what is shown, inviting a reshuffle

blocks.note: taken as written
the Roman numeral for one
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone is told to butt in for no real reason at all.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition completes an idiom: to put one's oar in is to interfere uninvited.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'put one's oar in' means to meddle or offer unwanted interference in other people's affairs.

clue.text: Heroic lines newfangled: "The c-crew did a bunk, but he nobly held on to the hose"

annotation.answer: THE BOY STOOD ON THE BURNING DECK WHENCE ALL BUT HE HAD FLED

indicators.note: the word does double duty: its first half, new, signals a fresh version, so the letters are made over into a different order

blocks.note: the second half of this word, after its signalling first half, joins the fodder

blocks.clueFragment: The c-crew did a bunk, but he nobly held on to the hose
blocks.note: the whole quoted sentence, letter for letter

explanation.surface: A mock-heroic news report: the stuttering crew fled while one brave lad clung to the fire hose.
explanation.walkthrough: The word newfangled splits: new is the signal and fangled joins the quotation as fodder. The answer opens Felicia Hemans's poem Casabianca, about a boy who stayed on his burning ship.
explanation.definitionFit: Casabianca celebrates a boy's courage in staying at his post, so its famous first line is verse about heroism.

clue.text: The setter's leitmotif

blocks.note: taken as written
the setter refers to themselves as me

explanation.walkthrough: The 's stands for is, joining the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A leitmotif is a recurring musical or literary idea, which is what a theme running through a work is.

clue.text: Scoop race entrants' urge to make love

blocks.note: to egg someone on is to urge them
to spoon is an old-fashioned word for to kiss and cuddle

explanation.surface: Runners in a race feel a sudden urge for romance.
explanation.walkthrough: An egg-and-spoon race is a children's sports-day event where runners balance an egg on a spoon.
explanation.definitionFit: The small scoop used for eating boiled eggs is the very implement carried by runners in an egg-and-spoon race.

clue.text: Swelling stops here

blocks.note: surface reading: the point where an inflammation ceases
setter's reading: a church instrument has a swell box and stops, both found together in it

explanation.walkthrough: A pipe organ has a swell, which controls loudness, and stops, which select sets of pipes; the clue also hints at a body part that might swell.
explanation.definitionFit: The keyboard instrument in churches has a swell pedal and drawstops, so swelling and stops are both features of it.

clue.text: Bottom employing this spacecraft?

blocks.note: first meaning: Bottom in A Midsummer Night's Dream is a weaver, and weavers pass the weft through the loom with this tool
second meaning: the reusable American orbiter

explanation.walkthrough: Bottom is Shakespeare's weaver, not a backside.
explanation.definitionFit: A weaver throws a shuttle across the loom, and NASA's reusable orbiter flown from 1981 to 2011 was the Space Shuttle.

clue.text: Pay no attention to this order

definitions.text: Pay no attention to this order

blocks.clueFragment: Pay no attention to this order
blocks.note: surface reading: ignore this instruction

blocks.clueFragment: Pay no attention to this order
blocks.note: setter's reading: a military command under which soldiers come out of the position called attention

explanation.walkthrough: On the parade ground, attention is a rigid posture; this command relaxes it, so the soldiers literally pay no attention.
explanation.definitionFit: Stand at ease is the drill command telling troops to relax from the attention posture, feet apart and hands behind back.

clue.text: Busy old England? On the contrary

blocks.note: standard abbreviation for England
aged means old
gives no letters: it tells you to put the two words the other way round, the country first

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether bygone England was a bustling place, then corrects themselves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the contrary' tells you to swap the order of the two words, so England comes before old.
explanation.definitionFit: A telephone line that is busy is described in Britain as engaged, and a person occupied with a task is also engaged.

clue.text: Underbids me possibly to take a load off

indicators.note: possibly hints that the letters shown are one option among many arrangements, so they are to be reordered

blocks.note: the eleven letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A bridge player hopes that underbidding will relieve them of a burden.
explanation.definitionFit: To disburden or disemburden is to free someone from a burden, removing weight or responsibility from them.

clue.text: Impatience with workers taking strides from a chap?

blocks.note: worker ants: the crossword's usual workers
strides is British slang for trousers, and wearing a chap's trousers puts one in his pants

explanation.surface: Restless labourers seem to borrow trousers from some man.
explanation.walkthrough: Strides is British slang for trousers; in British English pants can mean underpants, but in the idiom it means trousers.
explanation.definitionFit: Having ants in one's pants is an informal idiom for being fidgety, restless and unable to wait.

clue.text: See 5
Agent's message might call quietly for Fonteyn's comeback

indicators.note: a comeback is a return journey, so the dancer's first name is read in the backward direction

blocks.note: to cry is to call out
p, piano, is the musical marking for quietly
Margot Fonteyn was the great English ballerina

explanation.surface: A spy hints that he may quietly summon a celebrated ballerina out of retirement.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptogram is a text written in code or cipher, the kind of secret message a spy sends.

clue.text: Strikes against periodical seat reorganisation

indicators.note: a reorganisation puts things into a new arrangement, so these letters are set out afresh

blocks.note: Punch was the long-running British humorous magazine
taken as written

explanation.surface: Industrial action protests against a magazine rearranging its seating.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strikes' wants to be a noun about walkouts; it is a verb here.
explanation.definitionFit: To punch at someone is to aim blows towards them, which is to strike against them physically.

clue.text: How the cattle thief prepared dinner?

definitions.text: How the cattle thief prepared dinner?

blocks.clueFragment: How the cattle thief prepared dinner?
blocks.note: surface reading: the method a stock thief used to cook a meal
setter's reading: a cattle thief is a rustler, and the idiom for making a quick meal uses the same verb

explanation.walkthrough: To rustle up a meal is to make it quickly from whatever is to hand; rustling is also stealing livestock.
explanation.definitionFit: Rustled up is the idiom for knocking together food quickly, and rustling is what cattle thieves do to herds.

clue.text: To the French, Gaunt's rebellion brought such a golden age

definitions.note: the answer is an adjective describing such an age

indicators.note: a rebellion overturns the established order, so these letters are thrown into a new one

blocks.note: au is French for to the
taken as written, the possessive s included

explanation.surface: John of Gaunt's uprising against France supposedly ushered in a glorious era.
explanation.walkthrough: John of Gaunt was a powerful English duke of the 14th century.
explanation.definitionFit: The reign of the emperor Augustus was Rome's literary golden age, and Augustan names any comparable classical flowering.

clue.text: See 5
Twin of the King James Authorised Version

indicators.note: of here means made out of, so the letters are taken from inside the words that follow

blocks.note: the letters run from the end of James into the start of Authorised

explanation.surface: Someone names a twin edition of the King James Bible.
explanation.walkthrough: Fittingly, the answer is a Bible character, found inside the name of a Bible translation.
explanation.definitionFit: In Genesis Esau is Jacob's elder twin brother, who sold his birthright for a bowl of stew.

clue.text: Ingenious how gold turns up in the mine entrance

indicators.note: in a down entry, turning up means reading from bottom to top, so the letters go backwards
in places one piece inside the other

blocks.note: or is the heraldic word for gold
an adit is a horizontal entrance to a mine

explanation.surface: A miner explains how gold surfaces at the mouth of the pit.
explanation.definitionFit: Adroit means clever and skilful, especially with hands or tactics, close in sense to ingenious.

clue.text: See 5
Dithmithive polith here?

blocks.note: surface reading: lisping gibberish
setter's reading: a slurred line from a famous Scottish tongue-twister about a port's police dismissing us, used to test whether someone is drunk

explanation.walkthrough: The Leith police dismisseth us is a Scottish tongue-twister; said drunkenly it comes out like this. Leith is the port district of Edinburgh.
explanation.definitionFit: The tongue-twister names the police force of Leith, Edinburgh's port, so that place is where the slurred police are.

clue.text: Bound to lay off

blocks.note: first meaning: a boundary of shrubs around a field
second meaning: to offset a bet so as to limit losses

explanation.walkthrough: 'Lay off' looks like sacking workers; in betting it means spreading a risk.
explanation.definitionFit: A row of bushes marks a boundary, and bookmakers protect themselves by placing offsetting wagers, which is hedging.

clue.text: Dislodged one caught between, first, mother, then daughter

indicators.note: something between two halves of a word sits inside it

blocks.note: Eve, in Genesis the first woman and mother of all
Roman numeral for one
ct is a scorecard abbreviation for caught in cricket
standard abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: A family story: someone stuck between mother and daughter is pushed out.
explanation.definitionFit: To be evicted is to be forcibly removed from a home, which is what being dislodged means.

clue.text: See 5
See 5
Where two objects (all sublime?) were raised and inconclusively imposed

indicators.note: raising lifts things up and turns them over, so the two words are read backwards
inconclusively means without a conclusion, so the word loses its final letter

blocks.note: an object is an it, so two of them make two its
put means imposed, as a tax is put on goods

explanation.surface: A cryptic place-riddle quoting 'my object all sublime', a song from The Mikado.
explanation.walkthrough: The Mikado sings 'My object all sublime'; his opera is set in Titipu, and the setter's pseudonym Bunthorne is also from Gilbert and Sullivan.
explanation.definitionFit: Titipu is the fictional Japanese town where Gilbert and Sullivan's comic opera The Mikado takes place.
